content: In adults, the inconsistency in findings was downgraded once due to variability in point estimates, which showed overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 41%). This variability could not be attributed to small subgroups and may indicate moderate heterogeneity. Imprecision was downgraded twice due to the small sample size and limited number of events. Minor adverse events were reported in several studies. For example, Ushinohama (2016) noted dizziness in one participant, though the treatment group allocation was unknown. Yuan (2016) reported transient worsening of back pain (lasting up to one week), pain and bruising at acupuncture points, numbness and discomfort in the back and legs, as well as shoulder and foot pain. Kerr (2003) observed increased tenderness and leg pain for a few days following treatment. In another analysis, inconsistency was not downgraded as point estimates were in the same direction with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 0%). However, in a separate case, inconsistency was downgraded once due to point estimates moving in different directions, with some overlap in confidence intervals (I² = 71%), suggesting substantial heterogeneity that could not be explained by small subgroups. Meng (2003) did not specify the pain scale range, but it was assumed to be 0–10. Participants in this study had no leg pain, were from a highto upper-middle-income country, and were treated with Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) acupuncture combined with electrical stimulation. Several studies explored the effects of acupuncture and related interventions on chronic nonspecific low back pain. These included electroacupuncture, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, core stability training combined with acupuncture, and other complementary therapies. Adverse events were generally minor and transient, such as localized pain, bruising, or discomfort. The WHO guideline on the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults evaluated the benefits and harms of acupuncture compared to usual care. Critical outcomes included pain reduction, improvement in back-specific and general function, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, and adverse events. Evidence synthesis highlighted variability in study quality, sample sizes, and heterogeneity, leading to downgrades in confidence for some outcomes. Spinal manipulative therapy (SMT) was defined as any hands-on treatment involving movement of spinal joints, including high-velocity, low-amplitude manipulation and low-velocity mobilization. The evidence review for SMT also considered its benefits and harms compared to sham treatments or no intervention. Downgrades in evidence quality were often due to performance bias (lack of patient blinding), statistical heterogeneity, and small sample sizes. Massage therapy, broadly defined as manual manipulation of soft tissues to enhance health and well-being, was also reviewed. It included various traditional, complementary, and integrative approaches. The evidence suggested potential benefits for pain relief and improved function, though variability in study designs and outcomes was noted.
